package_info.package_name: Konni RAT Campaign (malicious document and payloads)
package_info.why_malicious: The package chain is designed to covertly deliver and execute a remote access trojan (RAT) on Windows systems, leveraging document macros, batch scripts, DLLs, and UAC bypass to gain persistence, exfiltrate data, and provide remote control to attackers. The campaign uses multiple stages to evade detection, escalate privileges, and maintain persistence, resulting in full system compromise and data theft.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: VBA script retrieves OLEFormat.IconLabel, writes to temp.zip, extracts, and runs check.bat with vbHide.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On document open (with macro enabled), the code extracts an embedded payload from the document, writes it to a temporary ZIP file, extracts its contents, and silently executes a batch script (check.bat) using hidden process creation, initiating the infection chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Macros that extract and execute files are a well-known initial access vector for malware, especially when execution is hidden from the user.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate documents should not execute hidden scripts or drop and run executables upon opening.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated document processing in highly controlled, trusted enterprise environments, but such behavior is extremely rare and tightly monitored.
key_indicators: Hidden process execution (vbHide)
Extraction and execution of embedded payload from OLE object
Creation and execution of batch script from document macro

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Batch script checks for remote session, OS version, architecture; renames DLLs; executes wpns.dll with parameters for UAC bypass.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the macro executes, the batch script checks the system environment (remote session, OS version, architecture), renames payload DLLs to evade detection, and launches the UAC bypass DLL (wpns.dll) with specific parameters to escalate privileges.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Batch scripts that manipulate DLLs, check system environment, and invoke UAC bypass techniques are highly indicative of malware staging and privilege escalation attempts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal batch scripts do not perform privilege escalation, rename DLLs, or prepare the environment for malicious payload execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate installers may check system architecture, but do not invoke UAC bypass or manipulate DLLs in this manner.
key_indicators: UAC bypass method selection and invocation
DLL renaming to evade detection
Execution of DLL with privilege escalation parameters

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DLL launches wusa.exe, duplicates its token, and uses CreateProcessWithLogonW to run netpp.bat with elevated privileges.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the batch script runs, the DLL abuses the trusted Windows binary wusa.exe to duplicate its token, then uses CreateProcessWithLogonW to launch the next batch script (netpp.bat) with elevated (SYSTEM) privileges, enabling privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Abuse of wusa.exe and token duplication for privilege escalation is a known malware technique to bypass UAC and gain SYSTEM-level access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs do not perform UAC bypass or launch scripts with duplicated tokens from system processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use case for this combination of token duplication and process creation via wusa.exe.
key_indicators: wusa.exe process launch for token duplication
CreateProcessWithLogonW API usage with duplicated token
Launching batch script with SYSTEM privileges

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Batch script stops netpp service, copies payloads to System32, creates/starts service 'netpp', adds registry keys for persistence, deletes traces.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After privilege escalation, the batch script stops any existing 'netpp' service, copies malicious payloads to the System32 directory, creates and starts a new Windows service named 'netpp', adds registry keys for persistence, and deletes installation traces to evade detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Installing unauthorized services, copying payloads to system directories, and manipulating the registry for persistence are hallmark behaviors of malware establishing long-term control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers do not create covert services with misleading names or erase installation traces to avoid detection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate software may create services, but not with misleading names or in conjunction with trace removal and unauthorized registry modifications.
key_indicators: Service creation with misleading or uncommon name ('netpp')
Copying DLLs to System32 directory
Registry modifications for persistence
Trace and evidence removal commands

execution_context.trigger: service start (system boot or manual start)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DLL loads API functions, decrypts C2 config from netpp.ini using AES-CTR, collects system info (systeminfo, tasklist), compresses and encrypts data, uploads to C2 via HTTP POST, fetches/executes C2 commands.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On service start, the DLL loads necessary API functions, decrypts the C2 configuration from netpp.ini using AES-CTR, collects system information and running processes, compresses and encrypts the data, uploads it to the C2 server via HTTP POST, and retrieves and executes further commands from the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated data exfiltration, encrypted C2 communication, and remote command execution are core behaviors of RAT malware, enabling attackers to control the system and steal sensitive data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate services do not communicate with external C2 servers, exfiltrate system data, or execute arbitrary remote commands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate service should perform encrypted C2 communication and arbitrary command execution based on remote instructions.
key_indicators: AES-encrypted C2 configuration file (netpp.ini)
System information and process list exfiltration
HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled endpoints
Remote command execution capability
Temporary file deletion after exfiltration

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Handles C2 commands: executes commands, downloads files, uploads files, processes base64/AES-encrypted payloads.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a C2 command is received, the DLL processes the instruction, executes arbitrary system commands, downloads and uploads files as directed, and handles additional payloads that are base64 or AES-encrypted, enabling full remote control by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Arbitrary command execution and file transfer on attacker instruction is the essence of RAT malware, providing attackers with persistent, covert access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate service should accept and execute arbitrary remote commands or transfer files on demand from an external server.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use case for arbitrary remote command execution and file transfer in a Windows service context.
key_indicators: Base64/AES-encrypted command processing
On-demand file upload/download via C2
Execution of arbitrary system commands from remote server

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious Word document and enables macros, triggering extraction of an embedded payload and execution of a hidden batch script.
Batch script checks system environment, renames DLLs, and launches the UAC bypass DLL to escalate privileges.
DLL abuses wusa.exe to duplicate a SYSTEM token and uses CreateProcessWithLogonW to launch the next batch script with elevated privileges.
Batch script installs the RAT as a Windows service ('netpp'), configures registry persistence, and deletes traces to evade detection.
RAT DLL loads on service start, decrypts C2 configuration, collects and exfiltrates system data, and establishes encrypted C2 communication.
RAT receives and executes attacker commands, enabling full remote control, file transfer, and ongoing data exfiltration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing attacker control and data theft

behavioral_signatures: Office document macro extracting and executing hidden batch scripts
Batch scripts renaming DLLs and launching UAC bypass modules
DLLs abusing wusa.exe and CreateProcessWithLogonW for privilege escalation
Creation of new Windows services with uncommon or misleading names (e.g., 'netpp')
Registry modifications for service persistence under SvcHost and Services keys
Automated exfiltration of system information and process lists
Temporary file deletion immediately after data exfiltration
Network communication to up.php and dn.php endpoints on suspicious domains
network_indicators: HTTP POST to up.php with parameter name=%PCNAME%
HTTP GET/POST to dn.php with parameters name=%PCNAME% and prefix
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents spawning hidden processes (such as cmd.exe or batch scripts), creation of suspicious Windows services (e.g., 'netpp'), and registry modifications for persistence under SvcHost or Services keys. Detect outbound HTTP traffic to known C2 domains (*.c1.biz) or to up.php/dn.php endpoints, especially with AES-encrypted payloads. Look for the presence of AES-encrypted configuration files (netpp.ini) and unusual use of wusa.exe for privilege escalation. Correlate temporary file creation and deletion with network exfiltration events to identify automated data theft.
